name: Dimensional Modeling & the Gold Layer
env: Runs here — DuckDB builds the gold-layer views live. (On the job this is Databricks Unity Catalog.)
goal: Turn the messy, query-by-query tables into a clean dimensional model a BI tool can sit on — facts, conformed dimensions, a date dimension, and a star schema (plus the snowflake variant and when each wins).

brief.body: The data room is great, but every query re-derives the same joins and cleaning from scratch — that doesn't scale, and we can't hand raw orders to a BI tool with duplicate customers and deprecated SKUs in it. Build us a proper gold layer: fact and dimension tables, a date dimension, clean keys. Then we (and Power BI) build on that, not on the swamp. I want a star schema — and I want you to be able to explain when you'd snowflake it instead.

clinic.title: Dimensional modeling in 5 ideas
clinic.body: (1) A fact table holds measurable events at a stated grain — here, one row per order. Facts hold numbers and foreign keys. (2) A dimension holds descriptive context you slice by — customer, product, date. (3) A star schema = one fact surrounded by denormalized dimensions (one join hop each). (4) A snowflake normalizes a dimension into sub-tables (Product → SubCategory → Category) — less redundancy, more joins. (5) A date dimension is non-negotiable: it powers every by-month/quarter/YTD slice. Medallion model: Bronze = raw (raw_web_events), Silver = cleaned (customers_clean), Gold = the dim_*/fact_* model you build now. The app has already created these gold views for you — the classwork shows exactly how.

classwork.title: Build the gold-layer star — together

steps.instr: dim_customer — reuse the clean view (already deduped/standardized in S1).
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW dim_customer AS
SELECT CustomerID AS CustomerKey, CustomerName, Segment, PrimeSubscriber,
  AgeGroup, Gender, City, State, Region, SubRegion
FROM customers_clean;
steps.checkpoint: One row per customer, no duplicates (inherits customers_clean's guarantee).

steps.instr: dim_product — add an explicit 'UNKNOWN' member so deprecated-SKU facts map somewhere instead of vanishing.
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW dim_product AS
SELECT ProductID AS ProductKey, ProductName, Category, SubCategory, Brand, Supplier, Rating FROM products
UNION ALL
SELECT 'UNKNOWN','Deprecated/Unknown SKU','Unknown','Unknown','Unknown','Unknown',NULL;
steps.checkpoint: 490 rows (489 products + 1 unknown member). Every fact row now finds a product.

steps.instr: dim_date — generate a contiguous calendar (not from strings). Note the DuckDB syntax; Databricks differs (see Spark note).
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW dim_date AS
SELECT d AS DateKey, year(d) AS "Year", quarter(d) AS "Quarter", month(d) AS MonthNo,
  strftime(d,'%b') AS MonthName, strftime(d,'%Y-%m') AS YearMonth,
  concat(year(d),'-Q',quarter(d)) AS YearQuarter, day(d) AS DayOfMonth,
  strftime(d,'%a') AS DayName,
  CASE WHEN isodow(d) IN (6,7) THEN true ELSE false END AS IsWeekend
FROM (SELECT unnest(generate_series(DATE '2022-01-01', DATE '2024-12-31', INTERVAL 1 DAY)) AS d);
steps.checkpoint: 1,096 rows (3 years incl. a leap day). Note: Year/Quarter are reserved words in DuckDB, so they're quoted. Spark form: explode(sequence(...)) + DATE_FORMAT(d,'yyyy-MM').

steps.instr: fact_sales — grain: one row per order. Route deprecated SKUs to 'UNKNOWN' so nothing is dropped.
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW fact_sales AS
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID AS CustomerKey, COALESCE(p.ProductID,'UNKNOWN') AS ProductKey,
  o.OrderDate AS DateKey, o.Quantity, o.Revenue,
  CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END AS NetRevenue,
  o.CostOfGoods, o.GrossProfit, o.Discount_Pct, o.ReturnFlag
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN products p ON o.ProductID = p.ProductID;
steps.checkpoint: 50,000 rows — exactly the order count, no fan-out. NetRevenue pre-computed so BI measures stay simple.

classwork.reference:
-- Validate referential integrity — every fact key must resolve (all zero):
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_sales f LEFT JOIN dim_customer d ON f.CustomerKey=d.CustomerKey WHERE d.CustomerKey IS NULL) AS orphan_customers,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_sales f LEFT JOIN dim_product  d ON f.ProductKey =d.ProductKey  WHERE d.ProductKey  IS NULL) AS orphan_products,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_sales f LEFT JOIN dim_date     d ON f.DateKey    =d.DateKey     WHERE d.DateKey     IS NULL) AS orphan_dates;

tickets.title: Validate the gold layer — shape & referential integrity
tickets.prompt: Prove the model is clean and correctly grained in ONE query. Return a single row with exactly six columns in order: dim_date row count, dim_product row count, fact_sales row count, then the three orphan-key counts (fact rows whose CustomerKey / ProductKey / DateKey don't resolve to a dimension). The three orphan counts must be zero. The gold views (dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date, fact_sales) are already created.
acceptanceCriteria: Single row, six columns in the stated order
Counts prove the grain: dim_date=1096, dim_product=490, fact_sales=50000
All three orphan-key counts are 0 (referential integrity holds)
hints: Use scalar subqueries: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dim_date), etc.
Orphans: LEFT JOIN fact_sales to each dim on the key, count rows where the dim key IS NULL.

tickets.title: Snowflake the product dimension
tickets.prompt: Normalize dim_product into a snowflake: dim_product → dim_subcategory → dim_category. Then write one sentence on why a star (denormalized) is usually preferred in Power BI despite the redundancy.
acceptanceCriteria: Three linked views with clean keys (CategoryKey, SubCategoryKey)
No category/subcategory text duplicated across the chain
hints: dim_category: DISTINCT Category. dim_subcategory: DISTINCT SubCategory + its CategoryKey.
dim_product_snowflake keeps only SubCategoryKey, not the text.
tickets.modelNote: Trade-off: 'Star wins in Power BI because the VertiPaq engine compresses redundant dimension text cheaply, and fewer relationship hops mean simpler DAX and faster filter propagation. Snowflake only pays off when a sub-dimension is huge or reused across many facts.'

tickets.title: A second fact: fact_web_events (constellation)
tickets.prompt: Build a cleaned fact_web_events (grain: one event) off the dirty clickstream, sharing dim_customer, dim_product and dim_date. This makes the model a constellation (two facts, conformed dimensions). Reuse your Sprint 5 cleaning.
acceptanceCriteria: Deduped by event_id, event_type normalized, timestamp parsed to a real date
DateKey = the event's date (joins to dim_date)
Guest events (NULL customer) routed to an 'UNKNOWN' member, not dropped
hints: DuckDB timestamp parse: try_strptime(event_ts,'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') across the 3 formats, COALESCE, cast to DATE.
tickets.solution:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW fact_web_events AS
WITH deduped AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS rn FROM raw_web_events),
cleaned AS (
  SELECT event_id, session_id,
    COALESCE(customer_id,'UNKNOWN') AS CustomerKey,
    COALESCE(product_id,'UNKNOWN')  AS ProductKey,
    LOWER(TRIM(event_type)) AS event_type,
    CAST(COALESCE(
      try_strptime(event_ts,'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'),
      try_strptime(event_ts,'%d/%m/%Y %H:%M'),
      try_strptime(event_ts,'%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
    ) AS DATE) AS DateKey,
    TRY_CAST(revenue AS DOUBLE) AS event_revenue
  FROM deduped WHERE rn = 1)
SELECT * FROM cleaned WHERE DateKey IS NOT NULL;
tickets.modelNote: A constellation only works if dimensions are conformed — dim_customer means the same to both facts. Don't build a second customer dimension. Spark uses try_to_timestamp(...) with 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss' style masks instead of DuckDB's try_strptime with strptime tokens.

tickets.title: Document the model: a Kimball bus matrix
tickets.prompt: Produce a Kimball-style bus matrix: a grid of facts (rows) × dimensions (columns) with a mark where a fact uses a dimension. It's how data teams communicate a model at a glance — a great portfolio artifact. Write it in the notes box.
acceptanceCriteria: Rows: fact_sales, fact_web_events (and fact_marketing if built)
Columns: date, customer, product, payment, event, channel
Shows which dimensions are conformed (shared) across facts
tickets.modelNote: Example — fact_sales uses date/customer/product/payment; fact_web_events uses date/customer/product/channel(utm); fact_marketing uses date/channel. Shared (conformed) dimensions — date, customer, product — are what let one dashboard slice every fact at once.
